newsitem.title: LIBERIA: U.S. to airlift W. African peacekeepers to Liberia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to airlift W. African peacekeepers to Liberia.

text.p: The United States is to provide further logistical back-up for the West African peacekeeping force in Liberia by airlifting in reinforcements from contributing countries, the commander of the force said.

General Victor Malu told Reuters late on Tuesday that the involvement of the United States would send a positive signal to the warring factions who have been disarming in preparation for national elections in May.

"U.S. logistics assistance will send a strong signal to former warring parties that the West African peacekeeping mission has the full support of a major world power," the commander of the Nigerian-led force said.

U.S. officials in Europe said that the United States is to provide four C-130 transport aircraft to fly in Malian and extra Ghanaian soldiers from Ivory Coast's commercial capital Abidjan to boost the 10,000-strong ECOMOG force by over 1,000.

"The arrival of the new troops is most timely. It will help us deploy more peacekeepers in populated areas so that politicians will have the confidence to campaign without fear of trouble," Malu said.
Neighbouring Ivory Coast, from where faction leader Charles Taylor launched the civil war in late 1989, is sending 90 medical personnel.

"The Ivorians are sending a medical team but this is very significant. It demonstrates to the former fighters and warring parties that West Africa as a whole is behind the peace process and that they have no place to hide," Malu said.
Taylor has already announced plans to contest the presidency in May, the date fixed under a peace accord agreed in August in Nigeria's capital Abuja. A dozen previous peace deals collapsed.
A meeting of West African army chiefs in Monrovia decided to recommend to regional foreign ministers meeting here on Thursday that elections should be held on schedule.

"Basically what we are recommending is the provision of security and disarmament and the going ahead with the elections," Nigerian chief of defence staff Major-General Abdul-Salam Abubakar said on Tuesday after a two-day review of disarmament.

Malu told the meeting on Monday disarmament had largely been completed, although his force needed more troops for tactical deployment in populated areas ahead of elections. "We have just completed the disarmament and demobilisation phases," he said.

Diplomats said that while there were still isolated cases of armed attacks and harassment in parts of the country, ECOMOG appeared in control overall and the security situation was expected to improve further before the poll time.
The United States has historic ties to Liberia, a nation founded by freed American slaves in 1847.

With the European Union, the United Nations and other agencies, it has stepped up logistical and material support for ECOMOG since an explosion of ethnic warfare in Monrovia last April and May nearly torpedoed the peace process.
Washington expects to spend up to $6 million to assist the organisation of elections.
U.N. and independent poll experts are less optimistic about the organisation of free and fair elections by May.
The war has killed well over 150,000 people.
